Food for the Future

By: Jana Marx | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tonight on Carte Blanche, witness how billionaire visionary Arturo Elizondo is revolutionizing the way we eat—by creating the world’s first egg without a chicken, and potentially changing the futu

Unique Selling Point:
The exclusive access Carte Blanche has secured to US-based visionary billionaire Arturo Elizondo, offering an unprecedented glimpse into his groundbreaking innovations and mission to transform the global food system.

Summary:
Arturo Elizondo is revolutionizing the global food system with his groundbreaking innovation, the chickenless egg. Raised in a small Mexican-American community in Texas, Arturo's journey from humble beginnings to becoming the founder and CEO of The EVERY Company is a testament to his unrelenting passion for sustainability and food security. With degrees in government and diplomacy from Harvard and experience working alongside U.S. Congressman Henry Cuellar, the USDA, and even interning for President Barack Obama at the White House, Arturo left the political arena to tackle a new frontier: protein production.
Armed with little more than ambition, Arturo moved to San Francisco to reimagine the future of food. Through The EVERY Company, he developed the world’s first animal-free egg, crafted using precision fermentation, which has already made its debut in Michelin-starred kitchens. This profile piece explores his relentless drive, the science behind his innovations, and how he’s reshaping how we think about food sustainability. Arturo's mission is clear: to democratize access to sustainable protein while preserving our planet for future generations. His story is one of disruption, determination, and hope for a greener, more sustainable future.

Further information:
Interactive baking session with the presenter: We will bake a beloved South African treat using the EVERY Egg white, while a traditional version is prepared in parallel. We will have local chef Enrico Persegani taste both versions and share his reaction.

Extra Budget Items:
*Venue hire TBC (Kitchen and lounge area for interview)

Script:


Chicken. Eggs. Beef.
These are the proteins we rely on every day.
But what if the very protein we depend on is unsustainable?
KEYNOTE_07:05 The way we make animal protein today is the number one cause of extinction on earth…It is the number one cause of deforestation, the number one cause of ocean dead zones and water pollution. 07:34 I decided that this is a problem that I wanted to dedicate my life to solving.
Meet Arturo Elizondo, founder and CEO of The EVERY Company.
“Hi, how are you? Good to meet you.”
We recently met this global food pioneer at the Singularity Summit, here, in Johannesburg.
14:53 I love this country. I love its people. One of the things that reminds me a lot of home is the pride culture, like Texas with our barbecue culture. The pride culture here is very strong, so there's a familiarity with that.
Number 2 is, I have found South Africans to be incredibly progressive, open-minded, and excited about potential, and that's very contagious.
With the global population reaching 8 billion and projected to hit 10 billion by 2050, our demand for protein is skyrocketing.
But can we keep up without breaking our planet?
Arturo thinks we can. He’s disrupting the world of protein.
07:00 Our protein can be used as a powder or a liquid. We’re an ingredient company.
And today, we’re going to put one of his inventions to the test.

Cooking Part 1 - Traditional Meringue

“So, Masa, if you have a look over here now…”
We’re in the kitchen with entrepreneur, chef, and former Koekedoor winner Corli Prinsloo, who says you don’t have to be a vegan or vegetarian to be concerned about the impact of food production on the environment.
CORLI 3:00 So I'm very open to alternatives because now your menu can still grow, and you can still get all the nutrition you need.
Meringues are the perfect way to showcase the essential role of eggs in a recipe.
Masa: “So Corli, today we’re going to make a meringue using real chicken eggs…and also, I must tell you I don’t know how to make meringue, so I’m really excited.”
Corli: “So I think we can start off by doing the egg whites.”
Masa: “And to be clear, we have 8 egg whites.”
Corli: “While we’re adding the sugar, it needs to melt…”
Corli: “Look at those nice peaks…”
Masa: “Ah.”
Corli: “This is going to go into the oven…”
Corli: “And of course, we have to fill this meringue.”
Corli: “We’re going to decorate it with some fresh fruit.”
Masa: “That looks beautiful.”
Corli: “Now you’ve got a lovely dessert for your guests.”
Masa: “Voila!”
We’ll see how Arturo’s replacement eggs shake up to Corli’s trusted recipe a little later.

Arturo’s Background and Motivation

The American entrepreneur and inventor was born near the Texas-Mexico border.
ARTURO I am one of six kids.
I grew up on the border between Texas and Mexico, actually on both sides.
Pause
ARTURO 2:40 I remember seeing kids my age in Mexico who had no shoes and were selling gum on the street. I realised that if I had been born a few miles south or to different parents, my life would have been completely different.
Driven by gratitude for his upbringing and a desire to make a difference, Arturo headed to Harvard University to study governance.
ARTURO 4:37 I ended up interning for my congressman in Texas, at the White House, and President Obama.
After experiences at the US Department of Agriculture and the Supreme Court, it was during a semester in Geneva that Arturo discovered his true mission—protein.

The Problem with Traditional Protein Production

Industrial farming is a race to meet the demand for food that we can’t win.
Arturo faced this fact in a news article 12 years ago.
ARTURO 6:14 The headline read:
“China has doubled its meat consumption in less than 20 years.”
As I kept reading, it discussed this broader trend globally.
07:24 We have this huge surge in demand year after year, and yet, we don't have the resources to keep up if we continue consuming as we are…
07:24 How are we not talking about this?
Factory farms, hidden from public sight, confine animals in cramped spaces with no sunlight, pumped with antibiotics and hormones…
…churning out proteins to meet demand but at devastating costs.
Animal protein production drives 80% of rainforest destruction, fuels 3 out of 4 new infectious diseases, and, according to studies, emits more greenhouse gases than the transportation sector.
ARTURO 9:16 A lot of it is because it's not just growing the animals; it’s all the feed.
PAUSE
I had NO idea (Masa: yeah) that our food system was doing this.
At just 22, Arturo packed his bags and set out to change the world of food—heading straight to San Francisco.
ARTURO 09:02 My parents weren’t happy because I was basically jobless, and I had no place to stay. What I told my mom and dad is, I’m going to give myself six months to see if I can make it happen. If not, then I’ll go back and get a real job.
19:03 I realised then that if I wasn’t going to be doing this, then who?
He came up with the idea of making egg proteins using a laboratory process instead of farming chickens.
20:36 Arturo first clip:
If we could help food companies be a little bit more sustainable, use a little bit less water, less energy, and use ingredients that don't have antibiotics or hormones, then we’d be making a difference.
Today, he brought us the world’s first egg white made without a chicken.
ARTURO 19:58 Part of why we chose egg proteins is because they are so incredibly functional. They're some of the most nutritional and functional proteins on the planet.

Cooking Part 2 - Introducing the EVERY Protein

Alternative proteins—often plant-based—are already on the market.
But this is something different.
Think of the process like brewing beer, but with a twist.
Arturo’s team takes the DNA 'recipe' chickens use to make egg proteins and, with a bit of fermentation magic, creates a product identical to real eggs.
But this egg white comes in powder form and doesn’t look anything like an egg. Will it act like one?
“We’ve had lots of eggs, right? And in place of those eggs, this is our special product, right?”
“Yes, that is indeed.”
“You can put it in our bowl.”
“You’re going to see, it has to dissolve, basically.”
“One of the nice parts, you know, of fermenting the protein instead of using chickens is there is no risk for salmonella.”
“It whisks quite fast and it’s very foamy.”
Masa 05:17 When you were thinking of this, where did you see it going?
Arturo: Well, my vision was, I don’t want to get my food from factory farms… Is there a way that we can have our cake—meringue—and eat it too, delivering an uncompromised experience? I think it’s something worth fighting for.
“Let’s slot this in the oven.”
“It really is a science, but here is our final result.”
“How pretty is this.”
“It’s science but also art.”
Corli: “At first, I must admit…I was a little bit sceptical… Like, how does this powder transform into something sustainable? As soon as I started whipping, it’s like I could not believe…”

Tasting

But the proof is in, well, the pudding.
Masa: So, are you ready to taste?
For an unbiased verdict, we’ve invited another chef for a blind tasting—one who doesn’t know the product and hasn’t seen the process.
Enrico Persegani, head chef and co-owner of SINN restaurant in Johannesburg.
We ask Enrico to compare the two versions of meringue.
STRAP
Enrico Persegani
Head Chef & Co-Owner | SINN
First, he tries the original.
Enrico: “It’s a little bit crunchy, and you can feel the airy side of it…also, the toppings are nice too.”
Corli: “I’m going to turn the plate for you, then you can taste the other one.”
Enrico: “Mmmm. Slightly more sweet… 2:19 So I believe the second one is the egg-free scenario. And the first one was the real one. Am I correct?”
“Yes!”
Our ratios may need some tweaking – but we can be forgiven, as this is the product’s first use in a South African recipe.
Enrico: “Oh wow, I’m gonna keep eating, yeah? I’m not gonna stop.”
There you have it—
Arturo is charting a new course for sustainable protein, proving we can reshape the future, one bite at a time.

But this egg white comes in powder form and doesn’t look anything like an egg. Will it act like one? “We’ve had lots of eggs, right? And in place of those eggs, this is our special product, right?” “Yes, that is indeed.” “You can put it in our bowl.” “You’re going to see, it has to dissolve, basically.” “One of the nice parts, you know, of fermenting the protein instead of using chickens is there is no risk for salmonella.” “It whisks quite fast and it’s very foamy.” Masa 05:17 When you were thinking of this, where did you see it going? Arturo: Well, my vision was, I don’t want to get my food from factory farms… Is there a way that we can have our cake—meringue—and eat it too, delivering an uncompromised experience? I think it’s something worth fighting for. “Let’s slot this in the oven.” “It really is a science, but here is our final result.” “How pretty is this.” “It’s science but also art.” Corli: “At first, I must admit…I was a little bit sceptical… Like, how does this powder transform into something sustainable? As soon as I started whipping, it’s like I could not believe…” Tasting But the proof is in, well, the pudding. Masa: So, are you ready to taste? For an unbiased verdict, we’ve invited another chef for a blind tasting—one who doesn’t know the product and hasn’t seen the process. Enrico Persegani, head chef and co-owner of SINN restaurant in Johannesburg. We ask Enrico to compare the two versions of meringue. STRAP Enrico Persegani Head Chef & Co-Owner | SINN First, he tries the original. Enrico: “It’s a little bit crunchy, and you can feel the airy side of it…also, the toppings are nice too.” Corli: “I’m going to turn the plate for you, then you can taste the other one.” Enrico: “Mmmm. Slightly more sweet… 2:19 So I believe the second one is the egg-free scenario. And the first one was the real one. Am I correct?” “Yes!” Our ratios may need some tweaking – but we can be forgiven, as this is the product’s first use in a South African recipe. Enrico: “Oh wow, I’m gonna keep eating, yeah? I’m not gonna stop.” There you have it— Arturo is charting a new course for sustainable protein, proving we can reshape the future, one bite at a time.

metadata.Summary: Arturo Elizondo is revolutionizing the global food system with his groundbreaking innovation, the chickenless egg. Raised in a small Mexican-American community in Texas, Arturo's journey from humble beginnings to becoming the founder and CEO of The EVERY Company is a testament to his unrelenting passion for sustainability and food security. With degrees in government and diplomacy from Harvard and experience working alongside U.S. Congressman Henry Cuellar, the USDA, and even interning for President Barack Obama at the White House, Arturo left the political arena to tackle a new frontier: protein production. Armed with little more than ambition, Arturo moved to San Francisco to reimagine the future of food. Through The EVERY Company, he developed the world’s first animal-free egg, crafted using precision fermentation, which has already made its debut in Michelin-starred kitchens. This profile piece explores his relentless drive, the science behind his innovations, and how he’s reshaping how we think about food sustainability. Arturo's mission is clear: to democratize access to sustainable protein while preserving our planet for future generations. His story is one of disruption, determination, and hope for a greener, more sustainable future.
